A_target.statement:
Let $\struct {S, \Lambda, \to}$ be a [[Definition:Labelled Transition System|labelled transition system]].
Then [[Definition:Bisimilarity|bisimilarity]] $\sim$ is the [[Definition:Greatest Element|greatest]] relation $R$ on $S$ such that:
:$R \subseteq \map F R$
where $\map F R$ is the set of pairs whose transitions can be matched with results related by $R$.

B_source.statement:
Let $\struct {L, \preceq}$ be a [[Definition:Complete Lattice|complete lattice]].
Let $F: L \to L$ be an [[Definition:Increasing Mapping|increasing mapping]].
Then $F$ has a [[Definition:Greatest Fixed Point|greatest fixed point]], given by:
:$\map {\operatorname {gfp} } F = \sup \set {x \in L: x \preceq \map F x}$

substitutions.the complete lattice: the powerset of pairs of states ordered by inclusion

object_map.reformulation: The definition of bisimilarity as 'the largest such relation' must be reformulated as a fixed-point equation before the lattice theorem gives its existence.

validity_conditions: F must be monotone with respect to inclusion, which holds because the matching condition is existentially quantified positively
the powerset of pairs must be a complete lattice, which it is under arbitrary union
the greatest rather than least fixed point is required, since the least one is empty
proof_plan:
Order the relations on $S$ by [[Definition:Subset|inclusion]].
The [[Definition:Power Set|power set]] $\powerset {S \times S}$ is a [[Definition:Complete Lattice|complete lattice]].

Define $\tuple {p, q} \in \map F R$ {{iff}}:
:$\forall p \xrightarrow a p': \exists q \xrightarrow a q': \tuple {p', q'} \in R$
and symmetrically for the transitions of $q$.
If $R \subseteq R'$ then $\map F R \subseteq \map F {R'}$, so $F$ is [[Definition:Increasing Mapping|increasing]].

By the [[Knaster-Tarski Theorem]], $F$ has a [[Definition:Greatest Fixed Point|greatest fixed point]]:
:$\displaystyle \nu F = \bigcup \set {R: R \subseteq \map F R}$

The [[Definition:Post-Fixed Point|post-fixed points]] $R \subseteq \map F R$ are exactly the [[Definition:Bisimulation|bisimulations]].
Hence $\nu F = \mathord \sim$.
In particular, to show $p \sim q$ it suffices to exhibit any bisimulation containing $\tuple {p, q}$, which is the [[Definition:Coinduction|coinduction]] principle.
{{qed}}
